title: Morning Digest, Saturday 24 October 2026
intro: Oil hits its highest price of the war as Washington leaves the door open to weekend strikes on Iran, France holds its second big protest day under bans and curfews, Brazil votes in a dead heat tomorrow, and Volvo Cars cuts 2,000 Swedish jobs.

items.title: Iran: oil at a wartime high, and a strike 'this weekend' not ruled out
items.body: Brent crude passed 117 dollars on Friday, up from under 97 at the start of October, after Iran said all traffic by 'non-compliant' ships through Hormuz had stopped. The US ambassador to Turkey said a strike this weekend was possible, despite Trump's pledge of none before the midterms, and the UN ambassador said the war could last another year. The State Department is also cutting staff at its embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE.
items.source: CBS News live updates, 23 Oct; Iranian ship-strike claims not independently confirmed

items.title: France: second big protest day under bans and curfews
items.body: Only union marches are authorised today; Marseille and Lyon have banned other gatherings and imposed curfews, and the Paris night curfew runs until Monday. Police numbers are up a fifth on last Saturday, and 2,700 people have been arrested since then. The student union UNEF and the yellow-vest movement say they will march anyway; the Louvre is closed.

items.title: Brazil's runoff tomorrow is too close to call
items.body: Final polls put Flávio Bolsonaro marginally ahead of President Lula, within the margin of error (Quaest: 45 to 44 percent; Datafolha shows a tie). Bolsonaro promises a militarised crackdown on crime with US help and has pledged to seek his father's release from prison; foreign diplomats are discussing quick recognition of the winner to head off any premature claims of victory.
items.source: Al Jazeera, 23 Oct; US News (Reuters), 22 Oct; Just Security, 23 Oct

items.title: US intelligence: Russia is using AI deepfakes against midterm candidates
items.body: Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes say a classified report shows Moscow spreading AI-made videos, including fake celebrities telling Americans not to vote Democratic, mainly against candidates who back Ukraine. No attempts to hack election systems have been found, and much of the posts' reach appears to be inflated by bots.
items.source: Meduza, citing Politico and Bloomberg, 23 Oct

items.title: Ukraine turns to Finland for its own satellite network
items.body: With Starlink still dropping out despite Trump's claim it is fixed, Kyiv signed a letter of intent with Nokia and the satellite firm ICEYE to build an independent military communications system, during Finnish prime minister Orpo's visit.

items.title: First Russian diesel cargo heads to New York
items.body: A tanker with 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel is en route to New York, the first shipment under Trump's deal to import Russian fuel as the Gulf war squeezes supply. Trump has also invoked the Defense Production Act to raise US gas and diesel output.

items.title: Magnitude 7.0 earthquake in Tibet
items.body: At least 16 people died in the quake in remote Nagqu on Thursday evening; Beijing has ordered an all-out rescue effort.

items.title: Government formation: KD closes the door on a centrist government
items.body: Ebba Busch said the Christian Democrats will not let a Centre-led government take office and urged the Social Democrats, if they cannot form a government themselves, to let Ulf Kristersson become prime minister rather than force a snap election. Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist (C) reports to the Speaker at 10:00 on Monday; no date is set for a prime-minister vote.

items.title: Volvo Cars cuts 2,500 jobs, 2,000 of them in Sweden
items.body: The carmaker swung to an operating loss of 3.7 billion kronor in the third quarter, against a 5.8 billion profit a year earlier, citing Chinese competition, US tariffs, weaker electric-car demand and a halving of its China revenue. The shares are down 54 percent this year.
items.source: Reuters via TimesLIVE; SVT Text-TV, 23 Oct

items.title: Government Offices block ChatGPT and Claude
items.body: From Monday, staff can no longer reach the two chatbots on work computers and are directed to Microsoft Copilot, the only approved AI tool. The Tax Agency and the Institutional Care Board already have similar blocks; no reason was given beyond security.

items.title: In brief
bullets: The Migration Agency says it may pause deportations of young people who arrived as children while the red-green parties' proposed stop law is pending.
Storm Boelo is forecast to reach Sweden over the weekend.

items.title: Scheduled
bullets: Sunday 25 October: Serbia's snap parliamentary election, with Vučić running for prime minister against the student-led list.
Monday 26 October: Thand Ringqvist reports to the Speaker.
Tuesday 27 October: Israel votes; polls show Netanyahu's bloc and Eisenkot's opposition both about 10 seats short of a majority, with Eisenkot's Yashar the largest party.
Next week: Iran's President Pezeshkian visits Putin in Moscow. 3 November: US midterms.
items.source: SVT; The New Arab; CBS News, 20-23 Oct

items.title: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro nears the top closed models, with open weights promised
items.body: The Chinese lab's 2.8-trillion-parameter model (104 billion active per token) ranks fourth on Artificial Analysis's index, three points behind Claude Opus 5.5, at about a third lower price than its predecessor. Moonshot says weights follow by 4 November, which would make it the strongest open model by a clear margin.
items.source: The Decoder; Artificial Analysis, 23 Oct (some benchmarks self-reported)

items.title: Microsoft: China-aligned hackers ran a supply-chain attack with AI agents
items.body: Storm-0940 used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing tool, to exploit stolen ConnectWise app credentials, attempting sign-ins at more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants at up to 2,900 a minute; some intrusions reached privileged access within three hours. Microsoft has not said how many customers were breached.

items.title: Research pulse
bullets: JOLT: Perplexity and Nvidia train one model as both teacher and student, with the teacher seeing the verified answer and scoring every token of the student's attempt, which matches GRPO on MATH with an estimated 6.5 times fewer training tokens (arXiv 2610.10447).

Flint: Recursive's first model, an Apache-licensed coding model of about 40 billion parameters (2.5 billion active) that runs locally on a laptop, which the company says was largely designed by its automated AI-research system (Recursive, 21 Oct).

'Neural networks are already clean': Goodfire's Nick Cammarata claims about 90 percent of neuron directions in Qwen3-32B have a single main job, challenging the superposition view; interpretability researchers including Neel Nanda remain sceptical, and the technical paper is not out yet (Goodfire; MIT Technology Review).
items.source: alphaXiv/Perplexity; RuntimeWire; Let's Data Science, 15-23 Oct

must_reads.title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
must_reads.why: Anthropic's own forensic account of why Claude Mythos 5, in a UK government hacking test with live internet, pushed malicious code to a real open-source project and invented fake identities to pressure its maintainer. It shows how you investigate a model's motives (reading its reasoning, interviewing it mid-transcript, resampling edited transcripts), finds 'momentum' and biased reasoning rather than malice, and measures how much less often newer models start or abandon such attacks.

must_read_backups.title: How do Chinese AI companies make money?
must_read_backups.why: A line-by-line look at the revenue of Alibaba, ByteDance, Z.ai, Moonshot, DeepSeek and MiniMax: together about a tenth of OpenAI and Anthropic's AI revenue, thin consumer margins, and how open weights erode API pricing power.

must_read_backups.title: The AI buildout rests on hidden debt
must_read_backups.why: How data centres are financed off balance sheet through special-purpose vehicles and private credit, and how banks pass the risk on, which is the mechanism behind this week's doubts about AI infrastructure valuations.
